questions.stem: The Olympic motto 'Citius, Altius, Fortius' — which of the following is the officially accepted English rendering adopted by the IOC?

options.option_text: Faster, Higher, Stronger — the official IOC English rendering
Swifter, Higher, Stronger — a commonly cited mistranslation
Faster, Stronger, Higher — order used in pre-1900 ceremonies
Higher, Faster, Stronger — version printed in early programs

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'Citius, Altius, Fortius' translates officially as 'Faster, Higher, Stronger' — adopted as the Olympic motto in 1894 and proposed by Henri Didon. Options B and D are wrong because 'Citius' means faster/swifter but 'swifter' is non-standard; option C incorrectly reverses 'Altius' (higher) and 'Fortius' (stronger). A fourth word 'Communiter' (Together) was added in 2021 but does not change the original three.

questions.stem: India competed as a newly independent nation for the first time at the 1948 London Olympics. In which sport did India win a gold medal at those Games?

options.option_text: Field Hockey — defeated Great Britain 4-0 in the final
Athletics — sprint events on the Olympic track
Wrestling — bantamweight freestyle at the venue
Shooting — men's rifle events held at the Olympic range

questions.explanation: A is correct: India's hockey team defeated the host nation Great Britain 4-0 in the final, winning gold at the 1948 London Olympics — the first Games India entered as an independent nation. Options B (Athletics) and C (Wrestling) are wrong; India's first individual track medal came from Norman Pritchard in 1900 as a British subject, and wrestling gold came much later. Option D (Shooting) is wrong; India's first shooting medal came only at the 2004 Athens Games.

questions.stem: Rajyavardhan Singh Rathore became India's first individual Olympic silver medallist at the 2004 Athens Games. In which specific shooting discipline did he compete?

options.option_text: 10m Air Rifle — stationary precision target indoors
Double Trap — two clay targets released simultaneously
Skeet — clay targets launched from different angles
25m Rapid Fire Pistol — five targets in timed sequence

questions.explanation: B is correct: Rathore won silver in Double Trap shooting at Athens 2004, where two clay pigeons are released simultaneously. Options A and D are wrong — 10m Air Rifle is the discipline Abhinav Bindra used for his 2008 gold, while 25m Rapid Fire Pistol is the event Vijay Kumar won silver in at London 2012. Option C (Skeet) is a different clay-target discipline where targets are launched from a single arc.

questions.stem: P.T. Usha missed the Olympic bronze in the 400m hurdles at the 1984 Los Angeles Games by just 1/100th of a second. Which country's athlete finished immediately ahead of her to claim bronze?

options.option_text: Romania — Cristieana Cojocaru edged Usha at the finish
United States — benefiting from the home crowd advantage
Soviet Union — dominant in women's track that decade
Jamaica — strong Caribbean sprinting and hurdles tradition

questions.explanation: A is correct: Romania's Cristieana Cojocaru clocked 55.41 seconds and PT Usha finished in 55.42 — a margin of 0.01 seconds. Option B (USA) is a tempting guess given home advantage, but the gold went to Morocco's Nawal El Moutawakel and USA's Judi Brown took silver; the USSR boycotted the 1984 Games (making C impossible), and Jamaica had no medallist in this event.

questions.stem: At the 2012 London Olympics, India achieved its best medal tally up to that point in history. Which option correctly states BOTH the total count AND the medal split?

options.option_text: 4 medals — 1 gold, 2 silver, 1 bronze (Bindra year)
6 medals — 2 silver and 4 bronze (no gold was won)
3 medals — 1 gold, 1 silver, 1 bronze (standard tally)
8 medals — 2 gold and 6 others spread across sports

questions.explanation: B is correct: India won 6 medals — silver for Vijay Kumar (shooting) and Sushil Kumar (wrestling), and bronze for Gagan Narang (shooting), Mary Kom (boxing), Saina Nehwal (badminton), and Yogeshwar Dutt (wrestling). Option A confuses this with Beijing 2008 when Abhinav Bindra won gold. Option C is too low, and option D (8 medals with 2 golds) overstates India's performance considerably.

questions.stem: K.D. Jadhav's bronze medal win at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics carries a distinction that no hockey team medal from 1948 onward could claim. What is that distinction?

options.option_text: It was India's first individual Olympic medal as an independent nation
It was India's first Olympic bronze medal in any discipline
It was the first Indian medal won without any government funding
It completed India's only full medal sweep in wrestling events

questions.explanation: A is correct: Jadhav won bantamweight freestyle wrestling bronze at Helsinki 1952, making it India's first INDIVIDUAL medal won by an independent Indian — the 1948 hockey gold and subsequent team medals do not qualify as individual medals. Option B is wrong because it was a bronze, not India's first medal in any discipline at all. Options C and D are fabrications — there is no documented funding angle, and India did not sweep wrestling medals.

questions.stem: India's men's hockey team won gold at eight Olympic Games between 1928 and 1980. Exactly how many of those eight gold medals were won BEFORE Indian independence on 15 August 1947?

options.option_text: Two golds only — 1928 Amsterdam and 1932 Los Angeles
Three golds — 1928 Amsterdam, 1932 Los Angeles, 1936 Berlin
Four golds — including the 1948 London Games as a transitional year
Five golds — team competed as British India right through 1952

questions.explanation: B is correct: India won Olympic hockey gold in 1928 (Amsterdam), 1932 (Los Angeles), and 1936 (Berlin) as British India — exactly three pre-independence golds. The 1948 London gold was won by the newly independent India (independence: August 1947; Games: July–August 1948), so it counts as a post-independence medal. Options C and D are wrong for including 1948 and beyond in the pre-independence count.
